# Multiple Comparisons Problem

### Comics

Look at the xkcd comics: https://xkcd.com/882/.
Do you see the problem?

### Simulations

Imagine that we have several treatments and we want to decide whether they all are the same or not.

We know how to compare two treatments: if the p-value given by a two-sample t-test is smaller than 
the chosen significance level, then we declare that the two samples are drawn from distributions with different means.
If both samples are drawn from some normal distributions, the percentage of wrongly declared differences 
will be approximately equal to the significance level:
```{r}
Simulation.Repeated <- 10000 # the number of times we repeat the simulation - affects accuracy of the results
repl <- 20 # the number of replications, n, also called the sample size
significance <- 0.05
n.errors <- 0 
for(i in 1:Simulation.Repeated){
  x1 <- rnorm(repl); x2 <- rnorm(repl); # generate two i.i.d. samples from the standard normal distribution

  # check if the samples have different means according to a t-test  
  if (t.test(x1,x2)$p.value < significance){
    # if the p-value is smaller than the significance level, 
    # then it is a Type I error (rejecting the null hypothesis, while it is correct)
    n.errors <- n.errors + 1
  }
}
print(paste0("The true p-value is ",n.errors/Simulation.Repeated),quote=FALSE)
```   

If we need to compare several samples, we can try to reduce the task to pairwise comparisons:
if there is a difference at all, then there should be (at least) one pair of different samples.

Let's find the true p-value (the percentage of errors) for this methodology.
Check whether among three samples all means are equal: 
```{r}
n.errors <- 0 
for(i in 1:Simulation.Repeated){
  x1 <- rnorm(repl); x2 <- rnorm(repl); x3 <- rnorm(repl); 
  # generate three i.i.d. samples from the standard normal distribution

  # check if any pair of the samples has different means according to a t-test  
  if (t.test(x1,x2)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x1,x3)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x2,x3)$p.value < significance
      ){
    # if the p-value is smaller than the significance level in at least one of the tests, 
    # then it is a Type I error (rejecting the null hypothesis that all means are equal, while it is correct)
    n.errors <- n.errors + 1
  }
}
print(paste0("The true p-value is ",n.errors/Simulation.Repeated),quote=FALSE)
```   

Check whether among four samples all means are equal: 
```{r}
n.errors <- 0 
for(i in 1:Simulation.Repeated){
  x1 <- rnorm(repl); x2 <- rnorm(repl); x3 <- rnorm(repl); x4 <- rnorm(repl); 
  # generate four i.i.d. samples from the standard normal distribution

  # check if any pair of the samples has different means according to a t-test  
  if (t.test(x1,x2)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x1,x3)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x1,x4)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x2,x3)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x2,x4)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x3,x4)$p.value < significance 
      ){
    # if the p-value is smaller than the significance level in at least one of the tests, 
    # then it is a Type I error (rejecting the null hypothesis that all means are equal, while it is correct)
    n.errors <- n.errors + 1
  }
}
print(paste0("The true p-value is ",n.errors/Simulation.Repeated),quote=FALSE)
```   

Check whether among five samples all means are equal: 
```{r}
n.errors <- 0 
for(i in 1:Simulation.Repeated){
  x1 <- rnorm(repl); x2 <- rnorm(repl); x3 <- rnorm(repl); x4 <- rnorm(repl); x5 <- rnorm(repl);
  # generate five i.i.d. samples from the standard normal distribution

  # check if any pair of the samples has different means according to a t-test  
  if (t.test(x1,x2)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x1,x3)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x1,x4)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x1,x5)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x2,x3)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x2,x4)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x2,x5)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x3,x4)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x3,x5)$p.value < significance |
      t.test(x4,x5)$p.value < significance 
      ){
    # if the p-value is smaller than the significance level in at least one of the tests, 
    # then it is a Type I error (rejecting the null hypothesis that all means are equal, while it is correct)
    n.errors <- n.errors + 1
  }
}
print(paste0("The true p-value is ",n.errors/Simulation.Repeated),quote=FALSE)
```   

For a larger number of samples, we need to perform more and more tests, but the main problem is the growth 
of the percentage of Type I errors. The latter is sometimes called ``p-value inflation''.

Do you see how this is related to the comics above?


# ANOVA and Around

First, let us repeat the simulations above using ANOVA omnibus F-test instead of pairwise comparisons:
```{r message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
library(reshape2)
```  

```{r}
Simulation.Repeated <- 1000 # ANOVA is heavier computationally, 10000 will take too long
n.errors <- 0 
for(i in 1:Simulation.Repeated){
  x1 <- rnorm(repl); x2 <- rnorm(repl); # generate two i.i.d. samples from the standard normal distribution
  data.wide <- data.frame(x1=x1,x2=x2)
  data <- melt(data.wide,measure.vars=c("x1","x2")) # aov() needs a data frame in the long format
  
  # check if the samples have different means according to ANOVA F-test  
  if (summary(aov(value ~ variable, data=data))[[1]]$`Pr(>F)`[1] < significance){
    # if the p-value is smaller than the significance level, 
    # then it is a Type I error (rejecting the null hypothesis, while it is correct)
    n.errors <- n.errors + 1
  }
}
print(paste0("The true p-value for 2 treatments is ",n.errors/Simulation.Repeated),quote=FALSE)
```   

```{r}
n.errors <- 0 
for(i in 1:Simulation.Repeated){
  x1 <- rnorm(repl); x2 <- rnorm(repl); x3 <- rnorm(repl); 
  data.wide <- data.frame(x1=x1,x2=x2,x3=x3)
  data <- melt(data.wide,measure.vars=c("x1","x2","x3")) 

  # Note that the syntax below does not change at all for more treatments  
  if (summary(aov(value ~ variable, data=data))[[1]]$`Pr(>F)`[1] < significance){
     n.errors <- n.errors + 1
  }
}
print(paste0("The true p-value for 3 treatments is ",n.errors/Simulation.Repeated),quote=FALSE)
```   

```{r}
n.errors <- 0 
for(i in 1:Simulation.Repeated){
  x1 <- rnorm(repl); x2 <- rnorm(repl); x3 <- rnorm(repl); x4 <- rnorm(repl); 
  data.wide <- data.frame(x1=x1,x2=x2,x3=x3,x4=x4)
  data <- melt(data.wide,measure.vars=c("x1","x2","x3","x4")) 

  if (summary(aov(value ~ variable, data=data))[[1]]$`Pr(>F)`[1] < significance){
    n.errors <- n.errors + 1
  }
}
print(paste0("The true p-value for 4 treatments is ",n.errors/Simulation.Repeated),quote=FALSE)
```   

```{r}
n.errors <- 0 
for(i in 1:Simulation.Repeated){
  x1 <- rnorm(repl); x2 <- rnorm(repl); x3 <- rnorm(repl); x4 <- rnorm(repl); x5 <- rnorm(repl);
  data.wide <- data.frame(x1=x1,x2=x2,x3=x3,x4=x4,x5=x5)
  data <- melt(data.wide,measure.vars=c("x1","x2","x3","x4","x5")) 

  if (summary(aov(value ~ variable, data=data))[[1]]$`Pr(>F)`[1] < significance){
    n.errors <- n.errors + 1
  }
}
print(paste0("The true p-value for 5 treatments is ",n.errors/Simulation.Repeated),quote=FALSE)
```   

### t- and F-distributions
Let us look at t- and F-quantiles first:
```{r}
qt(0.975,10)^2 # a two-tailed 5% t-quantile squared
qf(0.95,1,10) # a 5% F-quantile
qf(0.95,1,10:25) # the F-quantiles decrease (making the test more powerful) as the denominator df increase
```  

## Concrete Aggregates Example

An engineer is interested in how the absorption of moisture in concrete varies among five different concrete aggregates. 
Using a completely randomised design, 6 samples are to be tested for each aggregate.
The samples are exposed to moisture for 48 hours and the absorption of each sample is recorded 
in file `aggregates.csv` as shown below.

```{r}
print(agg <- read.csv("aggregates.csv"))
apply(agg,2,mean) # aggregate means
apply(agg,2,var) # aggregate variances
```  

### t-test 
We can compare aggregates 1 and 4 and then 2 and 4 using just t-tests and ignoring other observations:
```{r}
t.test(agg$AG1,agg$AG4,var.equal=TRUE)
t.test(agg$AG1,agg$AG4,var.equal=FALSE)
t.test(agg$AG2,agg$AG4,var.equal=TRUE)
t.test(agg$AG2,agg$AG4,var.equal=FALSE)
```  

### Long Format Transformation
```{r, fig.align='center'}
agg$rep <- 1:nrow(agg) # creating a case ID variable
print(agg.long <- melt(agg,id.vars="rep",variable.name="Aggregate",value.name="Absorption"))
agg.long$Aggregate <- factor(agg.long$Aggregate)
barplot(tapply(agg.long$Absorption,agg.long$Aggregate,mean),xlab="Aggregate",ylab="Absoprtion")
levels(agg.long$Aggregate) # check what treatments we have
replications(Absorption~Aggregate,data=agg.long) # get the number of replications and check that the design is balanced
```  

### ANOVA omnibus F-test

There are many functions for performing ANOVA analysis is R. 
The function `aov()` below is suitable for balanced designs only. 
```{r}
agg.model <- aov(Absorption~Aggregate,data=agg.long)
summary(agg.model)
```  
Here we are given the sum of squares for treatment \(85984\), 
the sum of squares for error \(88770\),
their respective degrees of freedom (\(4 = 5-1\) and \(25 = 5(6-1)\)),
the mean SSs, the value of the test statistics \(\tilde F = 6.054\)
and p-value \(0.0015\). 
We can confidently reject the null hypothesis that the absorption of moisture 
is the same for all five concrete aggregates.

# ANOVA assumptions

The examples below are just examples. You are encouraged to run the code on your own with different random seed 
to get more examples of possible plots etc.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
library(car)
repl <- 20 # the number of replications
n.trt <- 4 # the number of treatments (factor levels)
```   
We will consider a model where there are `r n.trt` treatments and the true treatment means are 
`r paste(1:n.trt,collapse=",")`, that is, the model is \(Y_{ij}= i + \varepsilon_{ij}\).

### Independent errors from the standard normal distribution

The errors are \(\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\).

```{r}
data <- data.frame(Response=rep(1:n.trt,each=repl) + rnorm(repl*n.trt),Treatment=factor(rep(1:n.trt,each=repl)))
```   
The `data` contains the "observed" `Response` for each `Treatment`, with `r repl` replications.
```{r, fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
summary(data.model <- aov(Response~Treatment,data=data))
plot(data.model,which=c(1,2,5),add.smooth=FALSE)
plot(data.model$residuals,main="Residuals vs Order")
leveneTest(data.model)
shapiro.test(data.model$residuals)
```   
The omnibus ANOVA F-test finds the difference very confidently.
All plots and tests are fine.

Note that we do not normally use a Residuals vs Order plot as in our examples the experiments are ordered 
by treatments and not in their actual order of experimentation. 
You should not use this plot for real-life experiments.

### Independent normal errors with different variances

The variance of errors depends on the treatment: \(\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,i^2)\).
```{r, fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
data <- data.frame(
    Response=rep(1:n.trt,each=repl) + rnorm(repl*n.trt,sd=rep(1:n.trt,each=repl)),
    Treatment=factor(rep(1:n.trt,each=repl))
  )
summary(data.model <- aov(Response~Treatment,data=data))
plot(data.model,which=c(1,2,5),add.smooth=FALSE)
leveneTest(data.model)
shapiro.test(data.model$residuals)
```   
Note that the unequal variances affected the Q-Q plot and the normality test as well, 
not only the directly involved Residuals vs Fitted Values and vs Treatments plots and
the homogeneity test.

Repeat for the same model of errors, just to see what may change for different random numbers:
```{r, fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
data <- data.frame(
    Response=rep(1:n.trt,each=repl) + rnorm(repl*n.trt,sd=rep(1:n.trt,each=repl)),
    Treatment=factor(rep(1:n.trt,each=repl))
  )
summary(data.model <- aov(Response~Treatment,data=data))
plot(data.model,which=c(1,2,5),add.smooth=FALSE)
leveneTest(data.model)
shapiro.test(data.model$residuals)
```   


### Independent identically distributed non-normal errors

First, try the uniform distribution on \([-1,1]\): \(\varepsilon_{ij}\sim U([-1,1])\).
```{r, fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
data <- data.frame(
    Response=rep(1:n.trt,each=repl) + runif(repl*n.trt,min=-1,max=1),
    Treatment=factor(rep(1:n.trt,each=repl))
  )
summary(data.model <- aov(Response~Treatment,data=data))
plot(data.model,which=c(1,2,5),add.smooth=FALSE)
leveneTest(data.model)
shapiro.test(data.model$residuals)
```   
The deviation from normality is detected, and that is all.


Second, let's look at a mixture of normal distributions \(\mathcal{N}(-2,1)\) and \(\mathcal{N}(2,2)\).
We will use an "honest" generation method: for each observation we randomly select one of the distribution
and then generate an error from this distribution
```{r, fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
DI<-sample.int(2,repl*n.trt,replace=TRUE) # the array of indices: which distribution is used for each observation 
data <- data.frame(
    Response=rep(1:n.trt,each=repl) + rnorm(repl*n.trt,mean=c(-2,2)[DI],sd=c(1,2)[DI]),
    Treatment=factor(rep(1:n.trt,each=repl))
  )
summary(data.model <- aov(Response~Treatment,data=data))
plot(data.model,which=c(1,2,5),add.smooth=FALSE)
leveneTest(data.model)
shapiro.test(data.model$residuals)
```   
Again, the deviation from normality is the only visible feature.


### Non-independent normal errors with variance \(1\)

First, consider a random walk model, 
where the expectation of the next error is equal to the current error: 
\(\varepsilon_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and 
\(\varepsilon_{k+1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon_{k},1)\),
where \(k\) is the experiment number.
This is a typical problem in experiments, which may occur if the same conditions are not restored before each experiment
(cleaning, re-adjusting scales, etc.).
As the errors now have an order, we cannot ignore the correct order of experiments any more,
so the order of treatments is randomised as well.

It is easy to see from the properties of normal RVs that the errors as above 
can be modelled by 
\(\varepsilon_{k}=\delta_{k}+\sum_{l=1}^{k-1}\delta_{l},\: \delta_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\)
```{r, fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
trt.order <- sample(rep(1:n.trt,each=repl)) # the order of treatments
data <- data.frame(
    Response=trt.order + cumsum(rnorm(repl*n.trt)),
    Treatment=factor(trt.order)
  )
summary(data.model <- aov(Response~Treatment,data=data))
plot(data.model,which=c(1,2,5),add.smooth=FALSE)
plot(data.model$residuals,main="Residuals vs Order")
leveneTest(data.model)
shapiro.test(data.model$residuals)
```   
The non-independence affects the Q-Q plot, but is mostly visible on the Residuals vs Order plot.


Now consider another model, more complicated,
where the next error is affected by the average of all previous errors
and the errors are dependent within each treatment only (this may happen 
if the treatments are somehow affected by each application,
for example, the "treatments" are human beings).
The model is 
where the expectation of the next error is equal to the current error: 
\(\varepsilon_{i1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and 
\(\varepsilon_{ij+1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\frac1j\sum_{l=1}^j\varepsilon_{il},1)\).

This model can be simulated by a for-loop,
but it is possible to obtain the following equivalent representation: 
\(\varepsilon_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+\sum_{l=1}^{j-1}\frac1l\delta_{il},\: \delta_{il}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\)
(one can prove by induction that this is the same as above).
```{r, fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
trt.order <- sample(rep(1:n.trt,each=repl)) # the order of treatments
errors.array <- sapply(1:n.trt,function(i){x<-rnorm(repl);x+cumsum(x/seq_along(x))}) 
# errors.array contains the errors for each treatment
errors <- 1:(repl*n.trt)
# the next line assigns errors in the order of treatments
lapply(1:n.trt,function(i){errors[trt.order==i]<<-errors.array[,i]}) -> unused.value 
data <- data.frame(Response=trt.order+errors,Treatment=factor(trt.order))
summary(data.model <- aov(Response~Treatment,data=data))
plot(data.model,which=c(1,2,5),add.smooth=FALSE)
plot(data.model$residuals,main="Residuals vs Order")
leveneTest(data.model)
shapiro.test(data.model$residuals)
```   
The most visible deviation is in the Residuals vs Fitted plot. 
Generally, violations of independence are very difficult to detect. 
This assumption must be provided by an appropriate design and conduct of experiments.

# Assumptions checking

We have three assumptions about the errors to check:

* independence
* homogeneity (equality) of variance
* normality

We do not have access to the true errors, so we use our model estimates to 
get residuals (the differences between the observations and the estimated treatment means)
and apply test to the residuals.

### Graphical tools

There are test for homogeneity of variance and normality assumptions. 
However, they have their own assumptions as well. 
Thus it is very important to use plots and assess whether there are any suspicious patterns.

```{r, fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
plot(agg.model,which=c(1,5),add.smooth=FALSE) # residuals vs fitted and vs treatments
plot(agg.model,which=2,add.smooth=FALSE) # Q-Q plot
```  
No visible patterns in any of the plots, hence we can proceed to the tests.

### Tests for homogeneity of variance

They are also called tests for constant variance or for equality of variances.
```{r}
bartlett.test(Absorption~Aggregate,data=agg.long)
leveneTest(Absorption~Aggregate,data=agg.long) # Brown-Forsythe test for the equality of variances
leveneTest(Absorption~Aggregate,data=agg.long,center=mean) # Levene's test for the equality of variances
leveneTest(Absorption~Aggregate,data=agg.long,center=mean,trim=0.1)
```   

Warning: there is another Brown-Forsythe test, for the equality of means, and 
it is the other test that is implemented in SPSS under this name. Beware!
```{r}
onewaytests::bf.test(Absorption~Aggregate,data=agg.long) # Brown-Forsythe test for the equality of means
```   

### Tests for normality

```{r}
shapiro.test(agg.model$residuals) # Shapiro-Wilk test
nortest::lillie.test(agg.model$residuals) # Kolmogorov-Smirnov / Lilliefors test
nortest::ad.test(agg.model$residuals) #  Anderson-Darling test
nortest::cvm.test(agg.model$residuals) #  Cramer-von Mises test
```  

## Assumptions violations

If we have found that assumptions are not met, 
we may still use ANOVA results, especially if the p-values are very small,
but with caution.

Alternative solutions are:

* use "non-parametric" tests (which have their own assumptions)
* transform the data (will be discussed later in application to linear regression)
* change the structure of the imposed model
* exclude some observations (outliers) or treatments

Let's consider the last two possibilities. 

### Treatments removal

A study of exposure to radiation in the home
used four different types of devices to measure the radiation levels: 
filter, membrane, open cup, and badge. 
Twenty devices of each type were placed in a chamber and subjected to constant radiation. 
The amount of radiation measured by each device was recorded.

```{r, fig.width=10,fig.align='center'}
radon<-melt(read.table("radon.csv",header=TRUE,sep=","))
names(radon)<-c("Device","Radiation")
summary(radon.model<-aov(Radiation~Device,data=radon))
plot(radon.model,which=c(1,2,5),add.smooth=FALSE)
bartlett.test(Radiation~Device,data=radon)
shapiro.test(radon.model$residuals)
```   
The equality of variances assumption is definitely violated.

Let's remove one unusual device:
```{r, fig.width=10,fig.align='center'}
summary(radon.model.reduced<-aov(Radiation~Device,data=radon[radon$Device!="Membrane",]))
plot(radon.model.reduced,which=c(1,2,5),add.smooth=FALSE)
bartlett.test(Radiation~Device,data=radon[radon$Device!="Membrane",])
shapiro.test(radon.model.reduced$residuals)
nortest::lillie.test(radon.model.reduced$residuals) 
```

Now the variances are fine, but it seems that the normality assumption is not met. 
However, the deviation from normality on the Q-Q plot is reasonably limited and 
the p-value of the ANOVA omnibus F-test is sufficiently close to zero to accept that 
there is a difference between treatment means indeed.


# Model estimates in R

We consider ANOVA model in the form \(Y_{ij} = \mu_i + \varepsilon_{ij}\). 
So far we discussed how to assess whether \(\mu_i\) are different. 
Another task is estimate \(\mu_i\) (and find confidence intervals etc. for them).
The ANOVA estimates for \(\mu_i\) is just the average of observations 
for the respective treatment:
\(\hat\mu_i = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n Y_{ij}\).
In R, these estimates can be computed as follows:
```{r}
tapply(agg.long$Absorption,agg.long$Aggregate,mean)
```   
and also using the following unnecessary advanced tools:
```{r}
coef(aov(Absorption~Aggregate+0,data=agg.long))
```   

However, the same model can be written in several forms, each convenient 
in some situations. 
The model above is called the means model. 


# Addendum: A non-parametric alternative test

An alternative to ANOVA omnibus \(F\)-test is Kruskal-Wallis test.
It does not require normality but does need the i.i.d. assumption.
Typically, the test is less powerful than ANOVA omnibus \(F\)-test,
and it is trickier to assess its assumptions.
```{r}
kruskal.test(Absorption~Aggregate,data=agg.long)
```
